b: The members of the firing squad have been selected, the rifles are ready to be loaded, as soon as the day dawns and the grave is dug, it will be my turn to act.

My brothers, all eleven of them, must scorn me, must think I am a weakling. And yet, of this whole boastful lot, only I am indispensable. We may look alike, we twelve standing in a gleaming, black, metallic row, the same, at least outwardly, but inside, ah, inside where it really matters, I am different, marked for a higher purpose.

Deride me all they want. Without me, their bullets would be forlorn, prone to blame themselves for what looms irreparably ahead. It is my existence and my existence alone—and lonely, so lonely—that liberates them from that fog of remorse.

When I was born—in a manner of speaking—plucked from the ranks of the polished steel cohort I had been part of till then, the Captain drilled into me the thick wad of my responsibilities and attributes. Yes, literally drilled, at the hour of my making, drilled, stuffed, patched a powderless plug into the core and shroud of my casement, rendering me incapable, henceforth, of causing harm. All the while praising me as he worked, this handsome, gallant officer calling me his little blank, his little cartridge, his favorite: You are not akin to the others, despite surface similarities in brand, build, heft, dark exterior, and elongated, aerodynamic design. That is the point, that nobody can tell from the outside that you are utterly unique and distinct—embrace the honor of your camouflaged, fusillade function, my little sweetheart, the battle-tested Captain insisted lovingly, smiling as he spoke, not for you to be discharged and propelled, not for you to feel the air bang open as you advance with steely speed, not for you the brief, shockwave satisfaction of impact, flesh that explodes, the eye socket pierced, the heart ripped apart, the taste of blood, the last cry, ah, you will not have to spend the rest of whatever wink of eternity is left to you recalling the nightmare of that last cry.

Sound and flash, yes, those you will enjoy, my Captain promised even as he was eviscerating my powder, emptying me of explosive filings, sound and flash and a reddish glow are essential so none of the soldiers who obey the order to fire know who you were allotted to, whether the bullet that dispatched the prisoner to the other world is theirs or is a dud, your performance of an ostentatious flare will be so masterful, your imitation of a true projectile and its recoil so perfect, your constricted muzzle so presumably primed and smoking, that each of those twelve human warriors can believe that he was the one to whom your safe, dull shell was randomly assigned, and therefore spared the heavy burden of having taken a life, and the life of one who was once and still is, still is, their friend, each of them can sleep a bit better this very night pretending that the live round was not his, just as each of them is praying, even now as the rifles are handed out and they find their place in line, they are praying—oh, I was once like them, the Captain says mournfully, confidentially, to me, to his favorite—they are hoping against hope, as I once did, that their weapon has been chosen as the one to be filled with innocence rather than ammunition.

Only you know who is to be the lucky, inert candidate, the Captain continues as he puts the last careful touches to his job, only you will remain irreplaceably behind, confined inside the barrel, watching your eleven brothers slice toward the young—young, alas so young—blindfolded deserter I have tied to the tree, the Captain says, motioning toward the field out there, just beyond the barracks, you will stay here inside the rifle, the Captain vows, saying goodbye to the real bullets as they whiz forward to say goodbye to the man who once was their own comrade, who ate rations with them and joked with them and exchanged fraudulent tales of nights of savage coupling in a brothel, I was once like them, you will have the privilege, my Captain declares, giving me one last pat, almost a caress, as he closes me off from any tampering, the privilege, he repeats, of assuaging the guilt of the executioners, only you know for sure who among them is faultless, only you know that when the trigger of the rifle where you lodge is pulled, no slug will be sent off, no shot gather momentum, no delivery, oh you are a marvel, my little faux cartridge, my favorite.
And with this last hymn of praise, he is done and, satisfied that I will not fail him, he departs to discharge his other duties.

And yet, now that he is leaving me to myself, now that my own thoughts begin to crowd out his pep and prep talk meant to bolster my bruised and locked ego, now that he is no longer present to console me for the inability to achieve some sort of manly fulfillment and release, now that his words are fading, certain suspicions start to creep into my marrow, tunnel into my shaft, ignite a question I cannot ignore: Am I that innocent, as the Captain has repeated far too often? Maybe he has harped on this over and over precisely because he deems that I am, in the last instance, guiltier than my brutal brethren. It is, after all, only my circumscribed presence alongside these eleven fully functional cartridges that allows the violation of air and flesh and space to smoothly come to pass, the lungs mutilated, the blasted body of the adolescent deserter whose only sin was to be afraid and want to return to his mother or his lover or his brother or his sister or his village, what if it is my presence, my alleviation of their responsibility, that is preventing this cluster of soldiers from sparking a rebellion, I am the one who stops them from shaking their heads and saying no, we will not be part of this travesty, firing into the clouds and sky, surging forward to free their doomed mate, untie his limbs from the tree, and disappear with him into the bright black night, what if I am the one blocking them from ceasing and desisting and challenging the whole machine of time and war and mud?

A fantasy. Of reconciliation and benevolence. My brother cartridges despise me, they lust to kill and kill some more, the soldiers who make up the squad feel betrayed by the young coward who deserted the company and left them in the lurch and recently made them dig a grave as the day began to break instead of catching some extra sleep before the next battle and bombardment descends upon them, they have as much contempt for him as the other bullets, the real ones, do for me.

But why then, if these combatants are so naturally disposed to violence, does the Captain now, dabbling in the poetic language I know so well, need to solemnly pledge to the assembled twelve that one of them will not carry the sunset and soul and payload of the dead man for the rest of his life, unless the Captain presumes—and fears—that they all harbor some deep-down dream of peace, a desire to evade imminent visions of that slumped, familiar body and the blood gushing forth?

And suddenly, now, right now, as the rifles are checked, each one, including the one into which I am about to be implanted, my imagination runs riot, I conjecture a more ominous, sickening possibility.

Have I been fooled by this cajoling Captain and his promise that I will be spared what the others are about to endure? Or more devious still, could he have secretly fed each of my eleven brother cartridges the same duplicitous origin story as mine, maybe they have also been told that they are dummy and blank and inoffensive, the better to relax them for the lethal, simultaneous duty ahead, so that each cartridge mistakenly considers itself harmless, just like me, just like me, and assures his respective recruit, just like me, just like me, to trust that the gods of carnage have favored his selection, whereas all, all of us, are equally dangerous, all of us are going to collectively commit this crime?

But this is not the moment, so late, so late, to surmise what my Captain may have whispered to my brothers, only I and no one else can decide what to believe, if the immaculate fate he augured for me is false or true. Ask myself, I must, I am compelled to as faltering, perhaps resolute, fingers slip me into the chamber: Would it not, after all, have been easier to lie to me, easier for him to concoct this fiction of my blamelessness than go to all the trouble of fabricating one special encasement and sabot, onerously getting rid of the live round and substituting a fake replica and caliber, what if my gunpowder was never extracted, my flight never gutted nor my barrel filled with wadding, maybe I will discover when the rifle is activated that I am expanding and speeding toward the objective, splattering straight into the brain of that young man tied to the eternity of that tree.
Can it be that I am not a blank, that I am carrying, just like all the others, a murderous charge?

No, no, this is too elaborate a trick, too cruel, too intricate, a waste of time, how could my Captain and maker be so conniving, why would he seem so fond of me, so saddened by his own memories, why go to such lengths to sweet talk and confuse me, the future is clear, my future . . .

And then I see it, that future. Not just the brother bullets heading for that young man’s body while I watch from my bloodless, sputtering perch but what comes next. None of them will miss the target, they are too scared of the Captain’s vigilance and too proud of their own prowess. A few will cross all the way through that bound body and out the other side into the tomb of the trunk of the tree, but most will find a permanent home inside the dead man himself, nestle intimately in a bone a kidney the spine the heart the heart, stay lodged there as the corpse is cast into the grave the soldiers have dug, most of the bullets will keep him company for as long as it will take the rain and the soil, the worms and the maggots, to do their job through hours and days and centuries. Outlasting the slowly decaying flesh, the steel of my brothers will not dissolve though millennia may transpire as they keep the victim and each other company in their fraternal foreverness, hosted and nursed by the man they have murdered, whereas I, whereas I . . .

Like the wrinkled remains of an aborted child I will be thrown away, no funeral rites for me, no blessings muttered over this stranger, that is the price that those of my kind must pay for not being like the rest, what awaits me in the requiem aftermath not included by the Captain in his story, that I will end up in a heap of solitary trash, unburied, unlamented, alone, so alone.

Would it not be better to be one of them? Join them at the conclusion of our voyage as we were joined at the beginning when a mother machine spat us metallically forth into the world, all of us again together?
There is no time to seek an answer.
I am abruptly stopped from this convoluted, whirling of envious twilight thoughts that lead nowhere.
Because soon, all too soon, I will know what my destiny is to be.

The Captain is inspecting the knots and rope that tie the prisoner to the tree, he lifts the blindfold to look into the man’s eyes, for an instant they light up like a candle in the dark of a house that will never again be inhabited and then are snuffed out as the rag descends, those eyes of his can no longer see or be seen.
He is barely older than a whip of a boy.

His mouth opens, is perhaps about to make a plea or call on some memory or mark the air that will soon be laden with bullets, his mouth opens but nothing is said, nothing is said, no final message for me, for us.
The drum rolls, the men are all lined up, the weapons are primed and they are ready and they are aimed, the Captain clears his throat for the final order.
I am one of the twelve.
Will I be like a seed that has ceased to believe that summer will ever come?
I am about to find out who I really am.
